headline: Threadit Community for 'People Who Peaked in High School But Moved On' Celebrates 5 Years of Healing
subheadline: r/FormerBigFish members share stories of finding identity beyond varsity jackets
summary: A Threadit support forum for former high school stars who have found peace with their current mediocrity marks a milestone anniversary.
content:
The Threadit community r/FormerBigFish is celebrating five years of helping former high school superstars come to terms with the fact that their best days might be behind them—and that's okay.

Founded by user @QuarterbackToAccountant in 2021, the subreddit has grown to 847,000 members who share stories of once being homecoming kings, star athletes, and debate champions who now live perfectly average lives they've learned to appreciate.

"I was literally voted 'Most Likely to Succeed' in 2008," wrote top post contributor @PeakedAt17. "I work at a call center now. And you know what? I'm happy. My coworkers don't expect me to carry them to state. The only pressure is hitting my call quota."

The community has developed its own terminology. "Peaking" refers to the high school glory years, while "valley walking" describes the difficult transition to anonymity. "Summit acceptance" is the final stage where members make peace with their trajectory.

"The hardest part was realizing nobody cares that I had 847 rushing yards senior year," shared @GridironToGrocery. "My coworkers don't even know what a running back is. It was devastating, then freeing."

Moderator @CheerCaptainToCPA has curated a wiki of resources including "How to Update Your LinkedIn Without Mentioning Prom Court" and "Conversations That Don't Involve Glory Days: A Guide."

The community explicitly bans what they call "glory posting"—sharing old achievements without connecting them to growth. "We're not here to reminisce," stated the rules. "We're here to release."

Psychologist Dr. Michael Torres called the community "genuinely therapeutic." He noted that unlike similar forums that wallow in past glory, r/FormerBigFish actively encourages members to find new sources of meaning.

"My therapist actually recommended this sub," wrote @ValedictorianToBarista. "Three years later, I don't introduce myself with my GPA anymore. I introduce myself with my sourdough starter's name. His name is Kevin."

The anniversary celebration included a virtual event where members shared current small victories. Top submissions included "I parallel parked on the first try" and "My houseplant survived a whole year."
author: Sandra Kim, Community Correspondent
